📉 The dashboard: The S&P 500 closed down 0.5%.

🔥 Today's stock spotlight: Intuitive Machines (+7.2%), the space company, said it received an "authorization to proceed" from an unnamed customer to start work on a $600 million, multisatellite communications infrastructure program.
 
 
1 big thing: OpenAI's power play
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

OpenAI announced a lease for a sprawling data center in central Ohio with financing partly guaranteed by Nvidia, saying it will create 35,000 construction jobs and 2,500 permanent operating positions.

  • Why it matters: The facility — which will be built and owned by SoftBank's SB Energy — illustrates the immensity of the computing and power needed to fuel the growth of the AI economy.

Zoom in: The data center will have 8 IT-gigawatts of computing capacity, powered by 10 gigawatts of new energy generation, on private land and federal property formerly used for uranium enrichment.

  • A massive 9.2 gigawatts of new gas-fired power is ultimately envisioned for the Ohio project — enough energy to power around 7 million homes, though estimates vary.
  • Nvidia — which will be the exclusive provider of chips to the site — agreed to guarantee up to $105 billion in conditional lease and power payment obligations to SB Energy, according to an SEC filing.
  • Nvidia also said today that it's investing $1.5 billion in SB Energy to back its "continued evolution into a leading AI infrastructure developer."

What we're watching: The deal may reignite fears of a "circular" AI bubble that could create systemic financial risks.

  • Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang took to X to try to head off the argument:
  • "Is this circular financing? No. OpenAI will pay the lease," he said, adding that Nvidia is using "its scale and long-term visibility to" enable the site to happen.

2. Anthropic surges
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

Anthropic's second-quarter revenue exploded from a year ago, helping push the AI lab's annualized revenue run rate above $65 billion ahead of its expected IPO, according to figures reported by Bloomberg.

  • The metric — an estimate of future annual revenue based on a short period of data — was hit at the end of July, per Bloomberg, and implies a sevenfold increase from where it was at the end of last year, Axios' Madison Mills writes.

What we're watching: Anthropic could go public before its rival, OpenAI.

  • IPOs would help the companies tap additional pools of capital to secure more capacity for model usage — and going first could give the Claude maker a leg up.

State of play: OpenAI's latest revenue run rate hit $40 billion, according to a message shared internally by co-founder Greg Brockman last week.

  • Caveat: The two companies may not measure revenue the same way.

Reality check: The "winner" of any metric used to measure where each company is in the AI race changes constantly.

4. Spirit's data afterlife
 

Illustration: Maura Kearns/Axios.
 

Google is acquiring Spirit Airlines' emails, calendar info, chats, documents, spreadsheets and other business data, according to a bankruptcy court filing.

  • It will use the data to improve its products and AI models.

Why it matters: Spirit Airlines ceased operations earlier this year after it failed to emerge from its second Chapter 11 bankruptcy, but attorneys are still handling the disposition of its assets.

Zoom in: Google won a bankruptcy auction for the data, agreeing to pay $10 million for the information.

  • The data does not contain any personally identifiable information, according to a court filing by PJT Partners vice president Dylan Friesner, an investment banker for Spirit.

By the numbers: The deal includes about 100 million emails and 500 million Microsoft Teams chats, according to a court filing.

  • It does not include passenger profiles or their frequent flyer information.

State of play: Google is expected to use the data as fodder for large language model training.

Now a major tourist attraction — in large part for the flying fish! — the market was originally created by the city after local farmers and consumers accused wholesale middlemen of price-gouging on produce. It's now one of the oldest continuously operated public farmers' markets in the U.S.
